items.title: Don Menza and Sam Noto interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 28, 1997
items.q: The interviewee mentions Charlie Parker only in the context of the interviewer's story about seeing a poster and hearing about a performance in Buffalo; the interviewee does not claim to have met, played with, or been directly influenced by Parker personally.

ctx.x: Did you feel like, I mean in listening to you play last night, it sounded to me like Dizzy Gillespie listened to you.

I don’t know about that. Dizzy was a good friend of mine. Then when I joined Kenton’s band, Dizzy was on that tour, it was a big package tour, and Charlie Parker was also. So I got to hear these guys for three months, every night. So I was hanging around with Dizzy. And there’s a lot of Dizzy in me. He was one of my first influences. And then of course then Miles and Clifford and Fats Navarro was a big influence. But you know it’s nice for you to say but it doesn’t work that way.
Well, in playing with Basie, did you have to alter your style some to fit that, or did it just seem to work?

items.title: Don Menza and Sam Noto interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 28, 1997
items.q: Even like the Charlie Parkers couldn’t make a living, who was, to me, one of the best or the best jazz player around ever.

ctx.x: Yeah. Anything he wants. A lot of wrong notes. He plays out of tune and that. And I didn’t hear that, what I felt was the spontaneity, the inventiveness of it and it was always exciting to hear three saxophones playing on the same horn, same mouthpiece, and they all sounded different. It just didn’t sound like twenty violin players sounding the same. And that isn’t quite true either, you know.

With me, I never thought of it as an art form or that, I just heard it and I said well this is what I want to do. And I thought if I got good enough at this, you know, I could possibly © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

make a living doing it, which was a big mistake you know. Even like the Charlie Parkers couldn’t make a living, who was, to me, one of the best or the best jazz player around ever. But I dug it. I mean there was some vital — something vital about it. It tells the whole story about life and I mean I just fell in love with it. And before that, I used to listen to Harry James as a great player and everything, but when the bebop thing came out, it changed my whole life you know? And I keep telling all these guys,…
